project_scope.note: All three current Monarda source concepts are installed learner cards. M. citriodora and M. punctata are project-range PASS; M. fistulosa is canonical learner-approved with range UNRESOLVED and remains excluded from confirmed-native metrics.

priority: calyx teeth and calyx-mouth hair pattern
annual versus perennial habit as supporting context
study_strategy.warning: Do not identify these Monarda from flower color alone. Start with stacked whorls versus a dense rounded terminal head, then bract and calyx structure. M. fistulosa range remains unresolved independently of learner admission.

quick_key.if: strongly interrupted/tiered whorls; purplish bracts and calyx teeth drawn into conspicuous long bristle tips
tiered whorls with pale bracts; cream/yellow corollas heavily purple-spotted; pointed non-bristled bracts; open ciliate calyx mouth
dense rounded terminal head rather than conspicuous stacked whorls; perennial habit; calyx throat densely hairy
quick_key.then: Monarda fistulosa — canonical learner card; range UNRESOLVED

visual_comparison.title: Monarda — compare the same plant part: bract → calyx → flower
visual_comparison.subtitle: Compare A versus B (floral bract tips), then C versus D (calyces). The named specimens are real, licensed exact-species photos; the arrowed parts match recorded original-image targets. Species-level taxonomy and county-range holds are unchanged.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: Do NOT choose by bract color or stacked tiers. Identify the actual two-lipped flower, then the BIG leaflike floral bract and the SMALL green calyx. A long thin bract awn usually favors lemon beebalm; shorter triangular calyx teeth usually favor spotted horsemint (check variety).

items.label: A · LEMON: long bristle-tipped bract
items.image_role: actual thin awn at tip of colorful floral bract
items.creator: Nadiatalent
items.caption: Yellowish/lavender corollas are actual flowers. Find the pointed pinkish bract UNDER the whorl: its apex is drawn out into a thin, conspicuous bristle. Look at the tip structure—not the bract color. This is LEMON BEEBALM.
items.why_it_matters: Flora of North Central Texas: citriodora bract apex abruptly ends in a bristle about 2–5 mm; punctata broad bracts are usually pointed without a terminal bristle.
items.photo_status: Reuses established species-level photo/arrow; regional key checked; mobile arrow position still needs browser QA.

items.label: B · SPOTTED: broad pointed floral bract
items.image_role: pink, pointed bract beneath spotted flower
items.creator: Alex Abair
items.caption: The broad purplish modified leaf hanging beneath the flower tier is a BRACT, not a petal. Its tip looks simply pointed rather than projecting as a long, thin bristle. This is SPOTTED HORSEMINT.
items.why_it_matters: Compare the same organ: leaflike floral BRACT tip vs lemon beebalm's more obvious extended bristle. Both have pink-purple forms.
items.photo_status: Reuses previously visually inspected locally saved punctata photo and supported arrow.

items.label: C · LEMON: long, finely pointed CALYX teeth
items.image_role: isolated ribbed calyx with long teeth and throat hairs
items.creator: Alex Abair
items.caption: This is a detached small GREEN CALYX, not the showy floral bract. Inspect a single projecting narrow tooth and the hairs around the calyx mouth. The teeth taper much farther than the triangular tips typical of M. punctata.
items.why_it_matters: The calyx is associated with ONE flower; lemon beebalm has long aristate calyx teeth, typically 2–7 mm in the published Texas key.
items.photo_status: Reuses established lemon species calyx photo and arrow, mobile QA pending.

items.label: D · SPOTTED: green ribbed CALYX below corolla
items.image_role: side view one spotted corolla and shorter green calyx
items.creator: Alex Abair
items.caption: Trace the curved pale-spotted COROLLA into its small GREEN RIBBED CALYX tube. That tube—not the big pink bract—has five teeth at the opening. The current photo is NOT same-scale with lemon's isolated calyx, so do not calculate tooth ratios by eye.
items.why_it_matters: Typical punctata teeth are shorter triangular/lanceolate, but Texas varieties vary in length. Calyx opening also helps separate Stanfield's beebalm; its white plug needs a rights-cleared macro.
items.photo_status: Reuses punctata verified photo/arrow; no inference about hidden mouth anatomy.

items.label: 1 · Lemon beebalm: flowering stems
items.image_role: whole flowering plant / repeated flower rings
items.creator: Clarence A. Rechenthin / USDA-NRCS
items.caption: Look from bottom to top of the stem: flowering rings (VERTICILLASTERS, crowded flower clusters at nodes) appear in distinct vertical tiers. At a distance the plant looks stacked, not like one continuous bloom.

items.label: 2 · Lemon beebalm: colored floral bracts
items.creator: Alex Abair
items.caption: Find the purplish LEAFLIKE BRACTS immediately beneath the small tubular flowers. Bracts are modified leaves, not petals or a calyx. Very fine aristate (bristle-tipped) calyx teeth remain a separate macro target.

items.label: 3 · Lemon beebalm: opposite foliage
items.creator: Nadiatalent
items.caption: Find two leaves opposite one another on the four-angled stem; next pairs may rotate ninety degrees (decussate). Use this as a MINT-family entry cue, not as species-only proof.

items.label: 4 · Spotted horsemint: stacked pale bracts
items.image_role: cream spotted corollas and pale showy bracts
items.creator: Alex Abair
items.caption: Differentiate the pale (sometimes pink or purple-tinged) LEAFLIKE BRACTS from the small yellowish COROLLAS extending above them. A purple spotted corolla is supportive, but unspotted taxa are documented; rely on architecture and calyx too.

items.label: 5 · Spotted horsemint: individual flowers
items.image_role: corolla / bract and upper leaf contrast
items.creator: Aaron Carlson
items.caption: Zoom in on a single COROLLA (joined petal tube with an upper and lower lip) above a broad pale BRACT. The strongly arched upper lip and purple spotting distinguish the flower parts from the much larger bracts. Do not interpret the whole colored tier as one bloom.

items.label: 6 · Spotted horsemint: botanical drawing
items.image_role: botanical line illustration / inflorescence and flower parts
items.creator: N. L. Britton & A. Brown (1913)
items.caption: This is a historical BOTANICAL ILLUSTRATION, not a photograph. Use its separately drawn leaf, floral, and calyx details for vocabulary. An exact arrow must wait until the detail's position is verified against the rendered illustration.

items.label: 7 · Wild bergamot: rounded head
items.image_role: rounded terminal inflorescence / many lavender corolla tubes
items.creator: Alex Abair
items.caption: The flowers form a fairly compact ROUNDED terminal head. Each projecting lavender 'tube' is one two-lipped flower, not a single petal. Compare with the more visibly separated tiers of lemon beebalm and spotted horsemint; calyx-throat hairs still need a macro.

visual_comparison.overlay_note: Both species have stacked flower tiers and can have purple dots. M. citriodora: longer bract awns and aristate calyx teeth; typical M. punctata: broad unawned pointed bracts, shorter triangular calyx teeth. Calyx photos are NOT matched to a common scale; do not claim numeric tooth ratios. Monarda stanfieldii requires a rights-cleared white-silver plugged calyx mouth photo, currently link-only.

look_here_first: FIRST compare the arrangement of MANY flowers: a rounded terminal head (M. fistulosa) versus separated vertically stacked flower rings (M. citriodora or M. punctata). SECOND find the SHOWY FLORAL BRACTS (modified leaves below flowers) and a SINGLE TWO-LIPPED COROLLA (the actual flower's joined petals). THIRD inspect the tiny CALYX TEETH and throat: lemon beebalm has markedly bristle-like bract/calyx tips; spotted horsemint usually has shorter nonaristate calyx teeth, usually cream-yellow purple-spotted corollas. Use color only as support.
shared_traits: Mint-family herbs with opposite (often decussate) foliage, square or four-angled stems, aromatic glandular foliage, and flowers in crowded heads or node-like whorls.
Individual flowers have fused, two-lipped (BILABIATE) corollas inside a persistent tubular CALYX; the conspicuous papery or green leaflike structures beneath flowering rings are BRACTS.

Monarda characteristically has two fertile stamens; recognize the four-lobed superior ovary yielding nutlets as common mint-family reproductive context, not a proved feature of current distant inflorescence photos.
The vertical rings are VERTICILLASTERS (clusters of small flowers arranged to resemble whorls); each colored tier is NOT one individual flower.

genus_diagnostics.inflorescence: Start with the SHAPE OF THE FLOWER CLUSTER: M. fistulosa usually has a more rounded dense terminal head, whereas M. citriodora and M. punctata more often show separated stacked flowering tiers. Architecture can vary; flowering habit alone is provisional.
genus_diagnostics.bract: A BRACT is a leaflike structure subtending flowers. Citriodora bracts are frequently purplish with conspicuous long bristlelike/aristate tips. Punctata bracts are conspicuous, frequently pale pink/white, but tips are usually not the same strongly aristate form. The currently installed photographs teach bract POSITION and COLOR; matched sharp tip macros remain missing.
genus_diagnostics.calyx: The CALYX is the ridged tubular cup of SEPALS surrounding the corolla tube, with distinct tooth tips and hair pattern. Compare the long awnlike tooth tips of citriodora with shorter pointed teeth and often open ciliate mouth of punctata; fistulosa has a densely hairy calyx throat. Existing general photos do not yet establish these minute differences.
genus_diagnostics.corolla: The COROLLA is the actual tubular two-lipped flower protruding from the calyx. Spotted horsemint usually shows cream-yellow corollas with purple speckles and strongly arched upper lip; lemon beebalm often has pale-to-lavender corollas; wild bergamot forms a head of slender lavender-to-pink corollas. Corolla colors overlap and variability exists.
genus_diagnostics.leaves: Look for OPPOSITE pairs of generally toothed lance-shaped leaves attached at mint-family stem nodes. Verify whether a colored part is a FLORAL BRACT rather than a normal stem leaf; color and leaf length are weak species separators.
genus_diagnostics.stem: The STEM is often FOUR-ANGLED, bearing opposite leaves. Monarda citriodora is commonly an annual and M. fistulosa a perennial; basal perennial growth is a supporting character, not a substitute for reproductive characters.
genus_diagnostics.fruit: Later seek the drying persistent calyx surrounding individual small NUTLETS, usually four from the deeply four-lobed ovary. No current installed three-species genus view verifies mature nutlets at macro scale: photo need remains.

comparison_cards.title: Lemon beebalm vs spotted horsemint
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Both can form stacked flower rings. Zoom to a showy bract (modified leaf) and the actual CALYX teeth, not just purple vs white bract color: citriodora often long BRISTLE-TIPPED, punctata shorter pointed. Spotted cream-yellow corollas support punctata; do not make corolla spotting absolutely required.
photo_requirements: matched frontal and side views of a tier
matched calyx and bract tips at same scale
comparison_cards.caution: Current installed photo set doesn't resolve calyx teeth at same scale; provisional without a macro.

comparison_cards.title: Wild bergamot vs stacked horsemints
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Fistulosa often forms one dense, ROUNDED terminal bee-balm head. Citriodora/punctata frequently show vertically spaced whorls with showy bracts. Compare whole flowering stems before a flower closeup.
photo_requirements: matched flowering stems whole inflorescence, full side profiles
fistulosa leaf node, calyx throat hair macro
comparison_cards.caution: Fistulosa is range UNRESOLVED in the project's 24-county evidence threshold; do not count as confirmed native.

comparison_cards.title: Is it a flower, bract, calyx or a flower whorl?
comparison_cards.look_here_first: A single two-lipped COROLLA is one flower; CALYX (joined sepals) is its little cup; the large papery BRACT is a modified leaf beneath flowers; many actual flowers are grouped into VERTICILLASTERS, commonly stacked in separated rings.
photo_requirements: open blossom with calyx and subtending bract plainly visible
verified arrows on exact structures when coordinates are checked
comparison_cards.caution: Botanical illustration is labeled as such and any future annotation must be verified.
